title: Kubernetes
subtitle: K8S MASTERY
description: Kubernetes is the industry-standard container orchestration platform. Learn pods, deployments, services, ingress, and beyond.

Kubernetes.desc: Kubernetes (K8s) automates deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications. Originally designed by Google, now maintained by CNCF.
Kubernetes.pricing: Free open source — pay for managed K8s (EKS, GKE, AKS)
Kubernetes.variants: Self-managed • EKS (AWS) • GKE (GCP) • AKS (Azure) • k3s • minikube
Kubernetes.freeTier: minikube / kind for local dev — free
Kubernetes.devNote: Start with minikube locally. Learn: Pod → Deployment → Service → Ingress. That's 80% of daily K8s.
Kubernetes.learn: Kubernetes is an automated operations team for your containers. It keeps your app running, scales it up/down, and recovers from failures — automatically.

Workloads.desc: The resources that run your containerized applications: Pods, Deployments, StatefulSets, DaemonSets, and Jobs.
Workloads.variants: Pod • Deployment • StatefulSet • DaemonSet • Job • CronJob
Workloads.devNote: Use Deployments for stateless apps, StatefulSets for databases, DaemonSets for node-level agents.

Pod.desc: The smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes. A Pod wraps one or more containers that share network and storage. Ephemeral — don't manage Pods directly.
Pod.devNote: Never create bare Pods in production — use Deployments. Bare Pods won't be rescheduled if a node dies.
Pod.learn: A Pod is a wrapper around one or more containers. Think of it as a logical host — containers inside share the same IP and can talk via localhost.

Deployment.desc: Manages a ReplicaSet to ensure a desired number of Pod replicas are running. Handles rolling updates and rollbacks declaratively.
Deployment.devNote: Set resource requests/limits on every Deployment. Use readiness probes so traffic only goes to ready pods.
Deployment.learn: A Deployment is a self-healing blueprint. Tell it: 'I want 3 replicas of this app.' It creates them, monitors them, and replaces any that die.

StatefulSet.desc: Like a Deployment but for stateful apps. Pods get stable network identities (pod-0, pod-1) and persistent storage that follows them across rescheduling.
StatefulSet.devNote: StatefulSets scale down from the highest ordinal. Always use PodDisruptionBudgets with StatefulSets.
StatefulSet.learn: StatefulSet gives each pod a permanent name and its own storage. pod-0 is always pod-0, even after restart.

DaemonSet.desc: Ensures a copy of a Pod runs on every (or selected) node. Used for node-level infrastructure: logging agents, monitoring, network plugins.
DaemonSet.devNote: DaemonSets automatically add pods to new nodes as they join the cluster.
DaemonSet.learn: DaemonSet = one pod per node, always. Like a security guard stationed at every building entrance.

Job.desc: Runs one or more Pods to completion. Guarantees a specified number of successful completions. Retries on failure.
Job.variants: Single job • Parallel jobs • Indexed jobs
Job.devNote: Set activeDeadlineSeconds to prevent stuck jobs from running forever.
Job.learn: A Job is a task that runs until done. Unlike a Deployment that runs forever, a Job runs, finishes, and stops.

CronJob.desc: Creates Jobs on a cron schedule. Kubernetes-native scheduled tasks. Uses standard cron syntax.
CronJob.devNote: Set concurrencyPolicy: Forbid to prevent overlapping runs. Set successfulJobsHistoryLimit to avoid job accumulation.
CronJob.learn: CronJob = cron + Kubernetes. Schedule: '0 2 * * *' means run at 2am every day. K8s creates a Job at that time.

Networking.desc: How pods communicate internally and how external traffic reaches your apps. Services, Ingress, DNS, and network policies.
Networking.devNote: ClusterIP for internal, LoadBalancer for external. Use Ingress to consolidate multiple services behind one LB.

Service.desc: A stable network endpoint for a set of Pods. Pods come and go but the Service IP stays constant. Four types: ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer, ExternalName.
Service.pricing: Free (LoadBalancer type incurs cloud LB cost)
Service.devNote: Use ClusterIP for internal services. Use LoadBalancer only for internet-facing services — each one provisions a cloud load balancer (costs money).
Service.learn: A Service is a permanent address for temporary pods. Pods die and get new IPs, but the Service IP never changes.

Ingress.desc: HTTP/HTTPS routing rules that expose multiple services through a single load balancer. Path-based and host-based routing. Requires an Ingress Controller.
Ingress.variants: nginx-ingress • Traefik • AWS ALB Ingress • GKE Ingress
Ingress.devNote: Install an Ingress Controller first (nginx is most common). Ingress resources do nothing without a controller.
Ingress.learn: Ingress is a smart front door. One load balancer, many services. /api goes to the API service, /app goes to the frontend.

NetworkPolicy.desc: Firewall rules for pods. Control which pods can communicate with each other and with external endpoints. Default: all traffic allowed.
NetworkPolicy.devNote: NetworkPolicy requires a CNI plugin that supports it (Calico, Cilium). Default K8s networking doesn't enforce policies.
NetworkPolicy.learn: NetworkPolicy is a bouncer for your pods. By default everyone can talk to everyone. Add a policy to restrict who can enter.

CoreDNS.desc: The default DNS server in Kubernetes clusters. Resolves service names to ClusterIPs. Every pod gets DNS configured automatically.
CoreDNS.devNote: Service DNS format: <service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local. Within same namespace just use <service>.
CoreDNS.learn: CoreDNS lets pods find each other by name. Instead of hardcoding IPs, your app connects to 'my-service' and DNS resolves it.

Storage.desc: Persistent storage for stateful workloads. PersistentVolumes, PersistentVolumeClaims, and StorageClasses abstract the underlying storage.
Storage.devNote: Use StorageClasses with dynamic provisioning — never manually create PVs in production.

PersistentVolume.desc: A piece of storage in the cluster provisioned by an admin or dynamically. Lifecycle independent of any Pod. Backed by cloud disks, NFS, etc.
PersistentVolume.devNote: Prefer dynamic provisioning via StorageClass over manually creating PVs.
PersistentVolume.learn: A PV is a storage unit in the cluster. Like a physical disk that's been registered with Kubernetes.

PersistentVolumeClaim.desc: A request for storage by a user. Pods use PVCs to request storage without knowing the underlying implementation.
PersistentVolumeClaim.devNote: PVCs bind to PVs based on size and access mode. With StorageClass, PVs are created automatically.
PersistentVolumeClaim.learn: A PVC is a storage ticket. Your pod says 'I need 10GB of storage' via a PVC. Kubernetes finds or creates a matching PV.

StorageClass.desc: Defines a class of storage with a provisioner. Enables dynamic PV provisioning. Different classes for SSD, HDD, replicated, etc.
StorageClass.variants: AWS EBS • GCE PD • Azure Disk • NFS • local
StorageClass.devNote: Set a default StorageClass so PVCs without a class get storage automatically.
StorageClass.learn: StorageClass is a storage catalog. 'fast' class = SSD, 'standard' class = HDD. PVCs pick a class and get the right disk.

Config & Security.desc: Manage configuration and secrets separately from application code. ConfigMaps, Secrets, RBAC, and ServiceAccounts.
Config & Security.devNote: Never hardcode config in images. Use ConfigMaps for config, Secrets for credentials. Enable encryption at rest for Secrets.

ConfigMap.desc: Store non-sensitive configuration data as key-value pairs. Inject into pods as environment variables or mounted files.
ConfigMap.variants: Env var injection • Volume mount • CLI args
ConfigMap.devNote: ConfigMaps are not encrypted. Never store passwords or API keys in ConfigMaps — use Secrets.
ConfigMap.learn: ConfigMap is a settings file for your app, stored in Kubernetes. Change the ConfigMap, restart the pod, new config applied.

Secret.desc: Store sensitive data like passwords, tokens, and keys. Base64-encoded (not encrypted by default). Enable encryption at rest for real security.
Secret.variants: Opaque • TLS • Docker registry • Service account token
Secret.alt: HashiCorp Vault • AWS Secrets Manager • KMS
Secret.devNote: Base64 is NOT encryption. Enable etcd encryption at rest. Better: use external secret managers (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) with the External Secrets Operator.
Secret.learn: A Secret is like a ConfigMap but for sensitive data. K8s keeps it separate and can restrict who can read it.

RBAC.desc: Role-Based Access Control. Define who can do what in the cluster. Roles, ClusterRoles, RoleBindings, ClusterRoleBindings.
RBAC.devNote: Follow least privilege. Start with no permissions and add only what's needed. Audit with kubectl auth can-i.
RBAC.learn: RBAC is the bouncer list for your cluster. A Role says what actions are allowed. A RoleBinding says who gets that Role.

ServiceAccount.desc: An identity for processes running in a Pod. Used to authenticate to the Kubernetes API and cloud services. Every pod gets a default ServiceAccount.
ServiceAccount.variants: Default SA • Custom SA • IRSA (AWS) • Workload Identity (GCP)
useCases: Allow pods to call K8s API
ServiceAccount.devNote: Use IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) on EKS to give pods AWS permissions without storing credentials.
ServiceAccount.learn: A ServiceAccount is a pod's ID card. It proves to the K8s API (and cloud services) who this pod is and what it's allowed to do.
